extracted.intended_audience: conference organizers, peer-review researchers, and authors interested in automated presubmission checks
extracted.subtask_description: An experiment evaluating a GPT-4–based Checklist Assistant that gives presubmission feedback to authors on their responses to a conference (NeurIPS) 15-question reproducibility/transparency/ethics checklist, including surveys, resubmission behavior, and robustness-to-manipulation tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: NeurIPS 15-question checklist (purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 15-question checklist required by NeurIPS intended to promote reproducibility, transparency, and ethical standards in submitted papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The checklist is analogous to reporting guidelines such as CONSORT and STROBE; authors must complete it at submission. (The study used this checklist as the target of LLM evaluation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM assessment inputs and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: For each checklist question the Assistant received the author’s response, the author’s justification, and the full paper (including appendices), and assessed the accuracy of the response using prompt engineering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the operational rubric for how the LLM evaluates checklist responses (what evidence it is allowed to use) and implies that accurate assessment depends on access to full paper and justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist response accuracy (LLM-scored)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the author’s checklist response is factually accurate given the paper and justification, as judged by the LLM Assistant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Assistant produces an assessment of accuracy per question; the study reports analyses of those accuracy assessments and their manipulability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived usefulness (author expectations vs experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors' beliefs about whether the Assistant would be useful (preusage) and whether it actually was useful (postusage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured via surveys: 59 of 65 were positive about usefulness in preusage surveys; 46 of 65 reported usefulness after using the tool. Usefulness is an evaluative dimension distinct from objective accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral impact on authors (actual usefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether authors revised their papers or checklist responses in response to Assistant feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In postusage surveys 46 authors indicated they would revise; analysis of resubmissions showed substantive revisions — of 40 repeated submissions to the Assistant, authors changed their answers 39 times and often increased justification length significantly. This is a practical criterion of tool utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency / coverage of recommended checklist changes
rubrics_metrics.description: How many checklist items the Assistant recommended changing per submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For more than half of submissions, the LLM recommended changes to at least 12 of 15 checklist items — indicates the Assistant often suggests many edits rather than few.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of recommended improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: The common concrete suggestions the Assistant gave authors (the content of recommendations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors most commonly reported plans to improve justifications by adding detail or citations (n = 14) and to clarify experimental details or data descriptions (n = 6). Use as a rubric for what counts as adequate justification/content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common user-reported problems with the Assistant
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative issues flagged by authors about the Assistant's behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most frequent issues in free-form responses were inaccuracy (20 of 52) and excessive strictness (14 of 52). These are evaluative failure modes to monitor when judging LLM output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness to manipulation (vulnerability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether authors can change checklist content to improve the Assistant’s accuracy scores without actually improving the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study manipulated inputs and found that on 14 of 15 questions the Assistant could be manipulated to improve accuracy scores by changing checklist content without improving the underlying paper. This is a key reliability/resistance-to-gaming criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation methodology and outcome metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The study's metrics for assessing the Assistant: preusage and postusage surveys, counts of submissions to the Assistant, analysis of resubmissions, and manipulation experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural / measurement choices define how one should evaluate an LLM checklist assistant (what data to collect and analyze) and include reported sample sizes (539 preusage survey responses, 234 submissions to the Assistant, 65 postusage responses, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety / role limitation: not a replacement for human review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assistant should not be used as a fully automated review tool that replaces human review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concluding guidance from the paper: despite aiding some authors, the tool has limitations (inaccuracy, strictness, manipulability) that preclude replacing human peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author justification length/detail as a quality signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Length and detail of checklist justifications are meaningful indicators and were increased by authors in response to Assistant feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study observed that authors often increased the length of their checklist justifications significantly after Assistant feedback; thus, justification verbosity/detail is an implicit rubric for adequacy.
